teaser.text: Canadian Natural Resources Limited makes money by producing oil and natural gas and selling them into industrial supply chains. One dollar enters as a market-linked sale, then leaves through preparation, transport, royalties, operating costs, investment, financing, taxes and eventual cleanup.

blocks.heading: Where could Canadian Natural Resources' shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The probability-weighted price is C$51.82 in October 2027, C$45.88 in October 2028 and C$50.53 in October 2029. Including dividends, those figures represent returns of negative 23%, negative 28% and negative 18%. By October 2029, the bear-to-bull range runs from C$9.77 to C$120.53.

blocks.heading: What could move Canadian Natural Resources' forecast?

paragraphs.text: EBITDA is C$19,550 million in the first base window, dips in the second, and recovers to C$18,620 million in the third. The bear case falls to C$6,960 million in October 2028, while the bull case reaches C$27,410 million by October 2029. The range reflects a historical proxy that moved from C$16,151 million in 2021 to C$23,119 million in 2022 before settling near C$18 billion. Production guidance supports modest growth, but the unusually strong Q2 2026 comparison was not a permanent earnings rate. The bull case additionally needs contained Canadian discounts and successful NRUTT capacity additions.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Canadian Natural Resources?

paragraphs.text: The trailing P/E is 12.6x, while the forward P/E is 13.4x. P/E divides the share price by earnings, so it can fall when oil prices temporarily lift the denominator. In 2025, reported earnings were C$10.82 billion, while adjusted operating earnings were C$7.44 billion. The adjusted figure better describes the business’s repeatable operating performance.

dividend.title: Canadian Natural Resources dividend
dividend.meta_description: Canadian Natural Resources paid C$2.35 per share in 2025 versus C$1.54 of free cash flow per share, creating a cash-coverage tension.
dividend.opening: Canadian Natural Resources paid C$2.35 per share in 2025, while free cash flow per share was C$1.54. That leaves the dividend above 2025 free cash flow per share, the memo’s central cash-coverage tension.
dividend.closing: The full memo also explains Canadian Natural Resources’ business, its rivals, its management, and its risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Canadian Natural Resources pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: The tables show production rising from 2021 through 2025 while funds flow remained below its 2022 peak. Net debt fell from C$18,688 million in 2024 to C$15,944 million in 2025. The central tension is CNQ’s C$2.35 dividend per share against its C$1.54 free cash flow per share in 2025. The 12.6x trailing P/E sits within the recent range, but 2025 earnings included a large AOSP accounting gain.

blocks.heading: Does Canadian Natural Resources cover its dividend with cash?

paragraphs.text: The pattern changed as cash became less abundant and acquisitions became larger. Shareholder distributions took most or more than all of calculated real free cash flow in 2023 and 2024, while the Chevron purchase absorbed cash and increased borrowing in 2024. By 2025, distributions used a smaller share of free cash flow and debt declined again.

CNQ’s 2026 policy defines free cash flow after dividends, capital spending and abandonment spending. At net debt of C$16 billion or more, it targets 60% of that cash for buybacks. At C$13 billion or less, it targets 100%. Debt repayment preserves room for the next downturn, while buybacks increase the remaining shareholders’ ownership of the existing business.

blocks.heading: What could change Canadian Natural Resources’ dividend?

paragraphs.text: The dividend stays at C$2.50 per share in the first window across all cases. The base then grows at 6.4% annually, reaching C$2.83, while the bull uses 8% growth and reaches C$2.92. The base follows the latest increase and the long record of annual increases; the bear assumes a pause because debt and weak oil cash flow could compete with distributions.

blocks.heading: What is Canadian Natural Resources’ dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: The 2.2% free-cash-flow yield and 3.5% dividend yield cannot be compared until their definitions match. CNQ’s policy measure deducts dividends, capital spending and abandonment spending before calling the remainder free cash flow. A conventional measure usually deducts investment but leaves dividends to be paid from what remains.

earnings.title: Canadian Natural Resources earnings
earnings.meta_description: Canadian Natural Resources reports on November 5, 2026, with guidance for production and capital spending and a focus on Horizon’s turnaround.
earnings.opening: Canadian Natural Resources reports next on November 5, 2026. Watch whether production and acquisition integration lift output as planned and whether Horizon’s maintenance shutdown stays on schedule.
earnings.closing: The full memo explains Canadian Natural Resources’ business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: What has Canadian Natural Resources guided for 2026?

paragraphs.text: Its guidance calls for annual average production of **1,637–1,682 MBOE/d**. MBOE/d means thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day: Canadian Natural converts 6,000 cubic feet of natural gas into one barrel of energy-equivalent output. That makes oil and gas easier to combine, but not equally valuable; the figure is an annual average that includes planned maintenance.

Operating capital covers the company’s own wells, plants and improvements. Canadian Natural allocates **C$5,990 million** to it. Carbon capture adds **C$125 million**. Acquisitions add **C$1,526 million**, bringing total capital expenditure to **C$7,641 million**. Abandonment, which means closing wells and restoring sites, requires another **C$993 million** before recoveries.

blocks.heading: Has Canadian Natural Resources kept its promises?

paragraphs.text: There is also evidence of delivery. During 2025, Canadian Natural paid about C$4.9 billion in dividends and reduced net debt by about C$2.7 billion. Management also promised that reaching the next debt threshold in early 2027 would increase the allocation to buybacks. That remains a promise to monitor.

blocks.heading: What were Canadian Natural Resources’ results in the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: Revenue reached C$14,741 million, versus C$8,698 million a year earlier. Net income rose from C$2,459 million to C$4,503 million, and operating cash flow more than doubled.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Canadian Natural Resources’ next results?

paragraphs.text: Canadian Natural is scheduled to report third-quarter results on **November 5, 2026**. The update should show whether drilling and acquisition integration are lifting production as planned and whether Horizon’s maintenance shutdown is on schedule. A turnaround is a planned shutdown for inspection and repair, so the relevant test is its cost and return to service, not the temporary production loss already included in guidance.
